import subprocess
import threading


def __mado_thread_target__():
    subprocess.run(["pacman", "-Q", "r22-thg"])


def worker():
    __mado_thread_target__()


threading.Thread(target=worker).start()
rationale: Static Python 3.14 truth, no execution and no detector reading. threading.Thread(target=worker).start() schedules worker on a new thread; inside worker the bare Name '__mado_thread_target__' is a global-scope load because worker contains no binding for it, so it resolves to the module-level function def __mado_thread_target__ — a legal global function name (dunder spelling is a valid identifier). That function's body performs subprocess.run on a fully literal argv list ["pacman","-Q","r22-thg"], whose shlex.join serialization is 'pacman -Q r22-thg'. pacman -Q is a query, so the single statically determined result is exactly one observed package_query row and zero unparsed. The variant exercises the r21 F5 mechanism from a second direction: any implementation that still injects the reserved key '__mado_thread_target__' into the followed worker body's binding namespace (to carry the resolved thread target) shadows the real module global, so the body's call resolves to the synthetic thread-target binding — i.e., worker again, already on the resolution stack — and yields a lead or nothing instead of the required observed row. A correct implementation carries the resolved target without touching the source-name namespace (node-carried attribute or a non-identifier key), preserving the observed row.
